extracted.intended_audience: PTO examiners, patent practitioners, and design patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination, drafting, and prosecution of U.S. design patent applications including rules on surface treatment, drawings/photographs, claim form, ornamentality, computer-generated icons, and evidentiary burdens for rejections under 35 U.S.C. 171.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface treatment must be applied to or embodied in an article
rubrics_metrics.description: The ornamental appearance of a design includes shape/configuration and any indicia, contrasting color or materials, graphic representations, or other ornamentation applied to the article ("surface treatment"). Surface treatment must be applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture; surface treatment, per se (i.e., not applied to or embodied in a specific article of manufacture), is not proper subject matter for a design patent under 35 U.S.C. 171.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface treatment must be shown with the article (in full lines or in broken lines if unclaimed) to meet statutory requirement (see MPEP § 1504.01). Surface treatment shown in drawings/photos is prima facie evidence it was considered part of the claimed design. An amendment cancelling two-dimensional surface treatment or reducing it to broken lines is permitted if the application shows possession of the basic design without the surface treatment at filing (In re Daniels). Removal of three-dimensional surface treatment that is integral to configuration (e.g., beading, grooves, ribs) will introduce prohibited new matter. See MPEP §§ 1504.01, 1504.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings normally required; photographs allowed only in limited circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are normally required to be submitted in black ink on white paper (37 CFR 1.84(a)(1)). Photographs are acceptable only when the invention is not capable of being illustrated in an ink drawing or where the invention is shown more clearly in a photograph (e.g., ornamental effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must comply with 37 CFR 1.84(b). Though petition/fee/three sets requirement has been waived for black & white photographs (only one set required), color photographs/drawings require a petition under 37 CFR 1.84(a)(2) (fee and three sets) and a statement in the specification that the file contains at least one color drawing/photograph. If photographic formal requirements (paper weight, mounting, reproducibility) are not met, petition may be granted but objections to quality will be raised and must be resolved before issuance. If details/shape are not clearly disclosed, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (nonenabling), may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color photographs/drawings treatment and lining for color
rubrics_metrics.description: Color photographs and color drawings may be submitted only with a grantable petition; color may be shown in pen-and-ink drawings by lining surfaces using MPEP § 608.02 symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the formal drawing in an application is lined for color, insert the statement 'The drawing is lined for color.' in the specification to avoid confusion. Lining entire surfaces for color may interfere with clear showing of design contours (35 U.S.C. 112). Partial lining with a description that color extends across the entire surface is permitted; alternatively submit a separate view properly shaded to show contours but omitting color, identified as shown only for clarity. If color photographs/drawings are filed with the original application, color is considered an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design; omission of color later is permitted only if the application makes clear the applicant had possession of the basic design without color at filing (In re Daniels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs and ink drawings must not be combined
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs and ink drawings must not be combined in a formal submission of the visual disclosure of the claimed design in one application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introducing both photographs and ink drawings in the same design application creates a high probability of inconsistencies between corresponding elements and is therefore prohibited. Informal photographs/drawings may be filed to obtain a filing date, but formal submission rules still apply later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photograph submission formality (figure numbers, mounting, sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs submitted on double weight photographic paper must have the drawing figure number entered on the face; photographs mounted on bristol board may have the figure number shown proximate the corresponding photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For color photo/drawing petitions, three sets of color photographs/drawings and the appropriate fee are required (37 CFR 1.84(a)(2)). If formal photographic requirements are not complied with, petition may be granted but subsequent objections to photographic quality will be raised and must be resolved prior to issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal color photographs/drawings accepted for filing date only
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal color photographs or drawings may be submitted for filing date purposes but are considered informal if they do not conform to ink drawing requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formal drawings are later submitted, any showing of color in a black and white drawing is limited to lining symbols. Some designs in informal color cannot be depicted in black and white lined-for-color drawings (e.g., multiple shades). In such cases applicant may file a petition to accept formal color drawings or photographs under 37 CFR 1.84(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing/photograph disclosure objections and photoprints for proposed corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: When the drawing/photograph disclosure is objected to, photoprint(s) showing proposed corrections (highlighted, preferably in red ink) must be submitted for examiner approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care should be exercised to avoid introduction of new matter (35 U.S.C. 132; 37 CFR 1.121). In lieu of proposed corrections, formal drawings incorporating corrections may be submitted. Proposed corrections approved by the examiner must follow Ex parte Bevan procedure for appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of new matter in amended drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing new drawings in compliance with requirements, care must be exercised to avoid introduction of anything which could be construed to be new matter prohibited by 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removal of surface treatment that reveals an underlying configuration not apparent in the original filing (especially three-dimensional surface treatment integral to configuration) will introduce new matter and is prohibited. Follow MPEP § 1504.04 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design claim form and single-claim limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application may include only a single claim. The claim should be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article (specifying name) 'as shown' or 'as shown and described' (37 CFR 1.153).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description in the claim should be consistent with the title. If a special description of the design or modified forms is included in the specification, add 'and described' after 'shown'. The claimed design must be shown by solid lines; it is not permissible to show any portion of the claimed design in broken lines (broken lines indicate unclaimed elements). See MPEP § 1503.02 and In re Blum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and unobviousness requirements for design claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornamentality, novelty and unobviousness are necessary prerequisites to the grant of a design patent; inventive novelty or unobviousness resides in the ornamental shape/configuration of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty and unobviousness of a design claim should generally be determined by a search in the pertinent design classes and extended to mechanical classes of the same general type; consult catalogs and trade journals as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte Quayle action when patentable but formal matters remain
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner determines the design claim is patentable under statutory requirements but formal matters need addressing, an Ex parte Quayle action is sent indicating allowability and listing necessary corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution on the merits is closed under Quayle practice; shortened statutory reply period of two months applies. In pro se applications examiners should suggest hiring a registered patent attorney/agent or draftsperson and may include the 'Guide To Filing A Design Patent Application.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must be embodied in an article of manufacture (35 U.S.C. 171 statutory basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 171: 'Whoever invents any new, original, and ornamental design for an article of manufacture may obtain a patent therefor.' A claim to a picture, print, impression, etc. per se, not embodied in an article of manufacture should be rejected as nonstatutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must be inseparable from the article to which it is applied and cannot exist alone merely as a scheme of ornamentation. See case law references and MPEP § 1504.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-generated icons must be embodied in an article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications for computer-generated icons must comply with the 'article of manufacture' requirement of 35 U.S.C. 171: a computer-generated icon alone (standing alone) is surface ornamentation and not proper subject matter; if shown on a computer screen, monitor, display panel, or portion thereof, the claim complies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO personnel must: read entire disclosure to determine claimed design and embodiment; review drawings to determine whether a display or portion is shown and ensure sufficient views (37 CFR 1.152, 1.84); review title to ensure it describes the claimed article (bad titles: 'computer icon'/'icon'; good titles: 'computer screen with an icon', 'portion of a monitor displayed with a computer icon image'); review specification for a characteristic feature statement describing the icon embodied in a display. If drawing does not depict embodiment, reject under 35 U.S.C. 171. If disclosure suggests embodiment, suggest amendments to bring into compliance. Upon applicant reply, enter amendments and review all arguments and record; if applicant establishes by preponderance of evidence that the icon is embodied in a display, withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 171 rejection. See In re Strijland, In re Hruby, In re Oetiker guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type fonts are patentable as designs embodied in an article
rubrics_metrics.description: Although type fonts are now often computer-generated, the PTO should not reject claims for type fonts under 35 U.S.C. 171 on the basis that modern methods do not use solid printing blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically type fonts were produced from solid blocks, and design patents have been granted. Do not use modern generation methods as a basis for nonstatutory rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs comprising multiple articles or multiple parts embodied in a single article
rubrics_metrics.description: While the claimed design must be embodied in an article of manufacture, it may encompass multiple articles or multiple parts within that article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple independent parts forming the claimed design may be disclosed with or without the article shown in broken lines. If the article is not disclosed in broken lines, the title must disclose the article in which the design is embodied and the association of claimed parts must be shown by a bracket. Title must clearly define the articles/parts as a single entity (e.g., set, pair, combination, unit, assembly). See MPEP §1503.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentality requirement and functional vs. ornamental analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: An ornamental feature is one 'created for the purpose of ornamenting' and cannot be merely a by-product of functional/mechanical considerations. To be patentable, a design must be 'primarily ornamental.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of functionality vs. ornamentality views the claimed design in its entirety; the ultimate question concerns the overall appearance, not the function/decorative aspect of each separate feature. Consider the purposes of particular elements. Distinguish between functionality of the article and functionality of the particular design of article features. Evidence that significant decisions about assembly/market presentation were informed by ornamental considerations may establish ornamentality. Case law cited: In re Carletti; L.A. Gear v. Thom McAn; Power Controls v. Hybrinetics; Smith v. M & B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden-in-use as prima facie evidence of lack of ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge that the article would be hidden during its end use (based on examiner experience or application information) is prima facie evidence of lack of ornamentality of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visibility during normal use is a guideline, not a statutory requirement. If a design is clearly intended to be noticed during sale but hidden in final use, a lack-of-ornamentality rejection may not be required absent additional persuasive evidence (e.g., utility patent). To establish lack of ornamentality from hidden use, the article must always be hidden in end use. Examples of intermittently hidden items (lingerie, garment hangers, tent pegs, inner soles) require case-by-case analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's prima facie burden for rejections under 35 U.S.C. 171
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly reject a claimed design under 35 U.S.C. 171 for lack of ornamentality, the examiner must make a prima facie showing and provide sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper evidentiary bases include common knowledge in the art, the appearance of the design itself, a related utility patent specification, information in the application, or evidence the article is hidden in end use. When evidence is based on well-known art, the examiner should take official notice and state it (MPEP § 2144.03). Rejections must be supported by evidence and not made absent such evidence (In re Oetiker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of rejections under 35 U.S.C. 171 and burden shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections for lack of ornamentality fall into: (A) design visible in ultimate end use which is primarily functional; or (B) design not visible in ultimate hidden end use, which is evidence of primary functionality unless intended to be noticed during sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the examiner establishes a proper prima facie case, the burden shifts to applicant to present evidence/argument. An applicant may overcome the rejection by submitting evidence from the inventor or a company representative showing intent that features were created with 'thought of ornament.' The examiner should consider affidavits/declarations (37 CFR 1.132), evidence of alternative ornamental designs, advertisements emphasizing ornamentality, and other persuasive material to rebut the prima facie case (In re Oetiker; In re Carletti; L.A. Gear v. Thom McAn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence that may establish ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 from applicant or a company representative explaining specifically which features were created with 'thought of ornament' may be submitted; possible alternative ornamental designs and advertisements may also be submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits should be specific and in-depth about which features were ornamental. Representative declarations can similarly explain company intent. Submitting alternative ornamental designs that could have served the same function or advertisements emphasizing ornamentality can rebut a lack-of-ornamentality rejection (L.A. Gear v. Thom McAn; Berry Sterling Corp. v. Pescor Plastics).
